content: Periostitis refers to inflammation of the periosteum, a layer of connective tissue that surrounds bone. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis should be performed in infants born to women with a reactive serologic test for syphilis (STS) under the following conditions: If the infant exhibits any clinical signs consistent with congenital syphilis. If maternal treatment was inadequate, unknown, or initiated late in pregnancy (after 20 weeks of gestation). If maternal treatment did not include penicillin. If adequate follow-up of the infant cannot be ensured. For other living infants diagnosed with confirmed or suspected congenital syphilis, a CSF examination should be conducted prior to treatment to establish a baseline for follow-up evaluations. While the necessity of CSF examination is debated, a quantitative Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL) test on CSF can provide meaningful results when combined with tests for elevated total protein and lymphocyte counts. The Rapid Plasma Reagin (RPR) card test should not be used for CSF evaluation. Regardless of CSF findings, all children diagnosed with confirmed or suspected congenital syphilis should receive treatment effective against neurosyphilis. Neonatal Treatment Although comprehensive and comparative data on neonatal syphilis treatment are limited, case reports have documented apparent treatment failures in infants treated with benzathine penicillin. This underscores the need for thorough evaluation of neonates to determine if they have occult active infection. The most appropriate treatment for active infection involves a 10-day regimen of either aqueous crystalline penicillin G or procaine penicillin G, rather than benzathine penicillin. Patients with neurosyphilis must be closely monitored with periodic serologic testing, clinical evaluations every six months, and repeat CSF examinations for at least three years. The possibility of reinfection should always be considered when retreating patients with early syphilis. A CSF examination should be performed before retreatment unless reinfection and a diagnosis of early syphilis can be definitively established. Retreatment should be considered under the following circumstances: If clinical signs or symptoms of syphilis persist or recur. If there is a sustained fourfold increase in the titer of a nontreponemal test. If an initially high-titer nontreponemal test fails to decrease fourfold within one year. Patients requiring retreatment should receive regimens recommended for syphilis of more than one year’s duration. Tetracycline is contraindicated in pregnant women due to potential adverse effects on the fetus. Erythromycin treatment during pregnancy is generally discouraged and should only be considered for patients with documented penicillin allergy (e.g., positive skin test or history of anaphylaxis) who are not candidates for penicillin desensitization. Clinicians opting for erythromycin treatment must ensure close clinical follow-up of both the mother and fetus to monitor for treatment failure. Maternal Treatment Follow-Up Pregnant women treated for early syphilis should undergo monthly quantitative nontreponemal serologic tests for the remainder of their pregnancy. Women who exhibit a fourfold rise in titer should be retreated. Treated women who fail to show a fourfold decrease in titer within three months should also be retreated. After delivery, follow-up is the same as for nonpregnant patients. Needed Studies Well-designed studies on the treatment of syphilis in pregnant women are urgently needed. Key areas of focus include: The transplacental pharmacokinetics of penicillin and other antibiotics. Treatment efficacy and ongoing analysis of treatment failure cases with current regimens. Evaluation of alternative regimens, such as benzathine penicillin G followed by high-dose amoxicillin/ampicillin with probenecid, particularly for secondary syphilis in late pregnancy. The role of HIV infection in cases of prenatal syphilis treatment failure. Syphilis in the Fetus and Neonate Diagnostic Evaluation For neonatal serologic testing, serum from the infant is preferred for both nontreponemal and confirmatory tests, as umbilical cord blood may yield false-positive results. After delivery and/or treatment, serial specimens should be used to monitor treatment efficacy or the degradation of transplacentally acquired maternal antibodies. When laboratory methods for fetal/neonatal-specific IgM treponemal determinations become widely available, serum will be the specimen of choice. Carefully controlled field trials will be necessary to guide their use in clinical practice. Microscopic Evaluation The placenta and umbilical cord are excellent sites for specimen collection for darkfield microscopy, immunofluorescence, and histological examination (e.g., H&E staining). Recommended Regimens for Symptomatic or Asymptomatic Infants Aqueous crystalline penicillin G: 50,000 units/kg intramuscularly (IM) or intravenously (IV) daily in two divided doses for a minimum of 10 days. Aqueous procaine penicillin G: 50,000 units/kg IM daily for a minimum of 10 days. For asymptomatic infants whose mothers were adequately treated with a penicillin regimen during pregnancy, treatment is not necessary if follow-up can be ensured. However, for asymptomatic infants whose mothers were adequately treated but whose follow-up cannot be ensured, many experts recommend a single dose of benzathine penicillin G (50,000 units/kg IM). Data on the efficacy of this regimen in congenital neurosyphilis are lacking. Therefore, if neurosyphilis cannot be excluded, the 10-day regimens of aqueous crystalline penicillin or procaine penicillin are recommended. Only penicillin regimens are recommended for neonatal congenital syphilis.
